lines.speaker: Fray Damaso
lines.text: You’ll see, when you’ve been here a few months you’ll be convinced of what I say. It’s one thing to govern in Madrid and another to live in the Philippines.

lines.speaker: Blond Man
lines.text: But—

lines.speaker: Fray Damaso
lines.text: I, for example, who can look back over twenty-three years of bananas and morisqueta, know whereof I speak. Don’t come at me with theories and fine speeches, for I know the Indios.

lines.speaker: Fray Damaso
lines.text: Mark well that the moment I arrived in the country I was assigned to a toxin, small it is true, but especially devoted to agriculture.

lines.speaker: Fray Damaso
lines.text: I didn’t understand Tagalog very well then, but I was, soon confessing the women, and we understood one another and they came to like me so well that three years later,

lines.speaker: Fray Damaso
lines.text: when I was transferred to another and larger town, made vacant by the death of the native curate, all fell to weeping, they heaped gifts upon me, they escorted me with music—

lines.speaker: Blond Man
lines.text: But that only goes to show—

lines.speaker: Fray Damaso
lines.text: Wait, wait! Don’t be so hasty! My successor remained a shorter time, and when he left he had more attendance, more tears, and more music.

lines.speaker: Fray Damaso
lines.text: Yet he had been more given to whipping and had raised the fees in the parish to almost double.

lines.speaker: Blond Man
lines.text: But you will allow me—

lines.speaker: Fray Damaso
lines.text: But that isn’t all. I stayed in the town of San Diego twenty years and it has been only a few months since I left it.”

lines.speaker: Fray Damaso
lines.text: Twenty years, no one can deny, are more than sufficient to get acquainted with a town. San Diego has a population of six thousand souls and I knew every inhabitant as well as if I had been his mother and wet-nurse.

lines.speaker: Fray Damaso
lines.text: I knew in which foot this one was lame, where the shoe pinched that one, who was courting that girl, what affairs she had had and with whom, who was the real father of the child, and so on.

lines.speaker: Fray Damaso
lines.text: for I was the confessor of every last one, and they took care not to fail in their duty.

lines.speaker: Fray Damaso
lines.text: Our host, Santiago, will tell you whether I am speaking the truth, for he has a lot of land there and that was where we first became friends.

lines.speaker: Fray Damaso
lines.text: Well then, you may see what the Indian is: when I left I was escorted by only a few old women and some of the tertiary brethren

lines.speaker: Fray Damaso
lines.text: and that after I had been there twenty years!

lines.speaker: Blond Man
lines.text: But I don’t see what that has to do with the abolition of the tobacco monopoly.

lines.speaker: Fray Damaso
lines.text: What? How’s that? Is it possible that you don’t see it as clear as day?

lines.speaker: Fray Damaso
lines.text: Don’t you see, my son, that all this proves plainly that the reforms of the ministers are irrational?

lines.speaker: Blond Man
lines.text: Do you really believe so?

lines.speaker: Fray Damaso
lines.text: Do I believe so?

lines.speaker: Fray Damaso
lines.text: As I believe the Gospel! The Indio is so indolent!

lines.speaker: Blond Man
lines.text: Ah, pardon me for interrupting you, but you have said something that awakens all my interest.

lines.speaker: Blond Man
lines.text: Does this indolence actually, naturally, exist among the natives or is there some truth in what a foreign traveler says

lines.speaker: Blond Man
lines.text: that with this indolence we excuse our own, as well as our backwardness and our colonial system.

lines.speaker: Blond Man
lines.text: He referred to other colonies whose inhabitants belong to the same race—

lines.speaker: Fray Damaso
lines.text: Bah, jealousy!

lines.speaker: Fray Damaso
lines.text: Ask Señor Laruja, who also knows this country.

lines.speaker: Fray Damaso
lines.text: Ask him if there is any equal to the ignorance and indolence of the Indio

lines.speaker: Señor Laruja
lines.text: It’s true.

lines.speaker: Señor Laruja
lines.text: In no part of the world can you find any one more indolent than the Indian, in no part of the world.

lines.speaker: Blond Man
lines.text: Gentlemen, I believe that we are in the house of an Indio. Those young ladies—

lines.speaker: Fray Damaso
lines.text: Bah, don’t be so apprehensive!

lines.speaker: Fray Damaso
lines.text: Santiago doesn’t consider himself an Indian

lines.speaker: Fray Damaso
lines.text: and besides, he’s not here. And what if he were! These are the nonsensical ideas of the newcomers.

lines.speaker: Fray Damaso
lines.text: Let a few months pass and you will change your opinion, after you have attended a lot of fiestas and bailúhan, slept on cots, and eaten your fill of tinola.

lines.speaker: Blond Man
lines.text: Ah, is this thing that you call tinola a variety of lotus which makes people—er—forgetful?

lines.speaker: Fray Damaso
lines.text: Nothing of the kind! You’re getting absurd.

lines.speaker: Fray Damaso
lines.text: Tinola is a stew of chicken and squash. How long has it been since you got here?

lines.speaker: Blond Man
lines.text: Four days

lines.speaker: Fray Damaso
lines.text: Have you come as a government employee?

lines.speaker: Blond Man
lines.text: No, sir, I’ve come at my own expense to study the country.

lines.speaker: Fray Damaso
lines.text: Man, what a rare bird!

lines.speaker: Fray Damaso
lines.text: To come at one’s own expense and for such foolishness! What a wonder!

lines.speaker: Fray Damaso
lines.text: When there are so many books! And with two fingerbreadths of forehead! Many have written books as big as that! With two fingerbreadths of forehead!
